claim: Pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants are associated with an increased risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
source: Pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants are associated with an increased risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: CDKN2A variants of uncertain significance (VUSs) are reported in up to 4.3% of patients with PDAC.
source: CDKN2A variants of uncertain significance (VUSs) are reported in up to 4.3% of patients with PDAC and result in significant uncertainty for patients and their family members as an unknown fraction are functionally deleterious, and therefore, likely pathogenic.
evidence: This prevalence is cited from published literature referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Twelve of the 29 CDKN2A VUSs were functionally deleterious (11 VUSs) or potentially functionally deleterious (1 VUS).
source: Twelve of the 29 CDKN2A VUSs were functionally deleterious (11 VUSs) or potentially functionally deleterious (1 VUS) and were reclassified as likely pathogenic variants.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the functional assay performed in this study.

claim: Over 40% of CDKN2A VUSs identified in patients with PDAC are functionally deleterious and likely pathogenic.
source: Thus, over 40% of CDKN2A VUSs identified in patients with PDAC are functionally deleterious and likely pathogenic.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental results showing 12 of 29 VUSs (41.4%) were functionally deleterious.

claim: The prevalence of pathogenic/likely pathogenic CDKN2A in patients with PDAC is increased to up to 4.1% when incorporating functionally deleterious VUSs.
source: When incorporating VUSs found to be functionally deleterious, and reclassified as likely pathogenic, the prevalence of pathogenic/likely pathogenic CDKN2A in patients with PDAC reported in the published literature is increased to up to 4.1% of patients, depending on family history.
evidence: This is calculated by combining known pathogenic variants with newly reclassified VUSs from published cohorts.

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has a median survival of less than 6 months.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a lethal cancer with a median survival of less than 6 months and a 5-year survival rate of only 10% (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from Siegel et al., 2020.

claim: PDAC has a 5-year survival rate of only 10%.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a lethal cancer with a median survival of less than 6 months and a 5-year survival rate of only 10% (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from Siegel et al., 2020.

claim: Surveillance of high-risk individuals has the potential to reduce mortality through detection of early, potentially curable, PDAC and its precursor lesions.
source: Surveillance of high-risk individuals (HRIs), such as people with a pathogenic germline variant in a pancreatic cancer susceptibility gene, for example, ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, CDKN2A, CPA1, CPB1, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, PRSS1, and STK11, has the potential to reduce mortality through detection of early, potentially curable, PDAC and its precursor lesions (Canto et al., 2018; Vasen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Canto et al., 2018 and Vasen et al., 2016.

claim: The International Cancer of the Pancreas Screening (CAPS) Consortium trials found that surveillance identified either PDAC or a high-grade precursor lesion in 6.8% of HRIs during a median follow-up 5.6 years.
source: The International Cancer of the Pancreas Screening (CAPS) Consortium trials found that surveillance identified either PDAC or a high-grade precursor lesion in 6.8% of HRIs, including relatives of patients with familial pancreatic cancer and individuals with a pathogenic germline variant in a pancreatic cancer susceptibility gene, during a median follow-up 5.6 years (24 of 354 individuals) (Canto et al., 2013; Goggins et al., 2020; Canto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from CAPS Consortium studies.

claim: In a screening study of 178 HRIs with a germline pathogenic CDKN2A variant, 13 individuals with PDAC were identified (7.3%) during a median follow-up 53 months.
source: Similarly, in a recent screening study of 178 HRIs with a germline pathogenic CDKN2A variant, 13 individuals with PDAC were identified (7.3%) during a median follow-up 53 months (Vasen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Vasen et al., 2016.

claim: The overall resection rate and 5-year survival rate in the CDKN2A screening study was 75% and 24%, respectively.
source: Importantly, the overall resection rate and 5-year survival rate was 75% and 24%, respectively (Vasen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Vasen et al., 2016.

claim: The CDKN2A gene encodes two proteins, p16INK4a and p14ARF.
source: The CDKN2A gene encodes two proteins, p16INK4a and p14ARF.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the CDKN2A gene.

claim: p16INK4a inhibits CDK4 activity and is a regulator of cell cycle progression and a tumor suppressor gene.
source: p16INK4a inhibits CDK4 activity, is a regulator of cell cycle progression, and a tumor suppressor gene (Serrano et al., 1993).
evidence: This is cited from Serrano et al., 1993.

claim: Pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants have been identified in up to 3.3% patients with familial pancreatic cancer.
source: Pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants have been identified in up to 3.3% patients with familial pancreatic cancer and up to 2.6% of patients with PDAC unselected for family history or without a family history of PDAC (Brand et al., 2018; Chaffee et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2018; Kimura et al., 2021; Lowery et al., 2018; McWilliams et al., 2018; McWilliams et al., 2011; Roberts et al., 2016; Shindo et al., 2017; Singhi et al., 2019; Zhen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: Pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants have been identified in up to 2.6% of patients with PDAC unselected for family history or without a family history of PDAC.
source: Pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants have been identified in up to 3.3% patients with familial pancreatic cancer and up to 2.6% of patients with PDAC unselected for family history or without a family history of PDAC (Brand et al., 2018; Chaffee et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2018; Kimura et al., 2021; Lowery et al., 2018; McWilliams et al., 2018; McWilliams et al., 2011; Roberts et al., 2016; Shindo et al., 2017; Singhi et al., 2019; Zhen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: Individuals with a known pathogenic germline CDKN2A variant have up to a 12.3-fold increased risk of developing PDAC.
source: Strikingly, individuals with a known pathogenic germline CDKN2A variant have up to a 12.3-fold increased risk of developing PDAC (Hu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Hu et al., 2018.

claim: Germline CDKN2A VUSs are found in 2.9–4.3% of patients with PDAC, depending on family history.
source: CDKN2A VUSs, predominantly rare missense variants, are found in 2.9–4.3% of patients with PDAC, depending on family history (Chaffee et al., 2018; McWilliams et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2016; Shindo et al., 2017; Zhen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: Individuals with a pathogenic germline CDKN2A variant are recommended for clinical surveillance.
source: For example, while individuals with a pathogenic germline CDKN2A variant are recommended for clinical surveillance, those with a germline CDKN2A VUS are often not included in surveillance studies unless they fulfill family history criteria (Goggins et al., 2020; Stoffel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from clinical guidelines (Goggins et al., 2020; Stoffel et al., 2019).

claim: Individuals with a germline CDKN2A VUS are often not included in surveillance studies unless they fulfill family history criteria.
source: For example, while individuals with a pathogenic germline CDKN2A variant are recommended for clinical surveillance, those with a germline CDKN2A VUS are often not included in surveillance studies unless they fulfill family history criteria (Goggins et al., 2020; Stoffel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from clinical guidelines (Goggins et al., 2020; Stoffel et al., 2019).

claim: The positive and negative predictive values for assays of broad cellular function are higher than those considering only CDK4/6 binding.
source: The positive and negative predictive values for assays of broad cellular function are higher than those considering only CDK4/6 binding (Miller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Miller et al., 2011.

claim: Some CDKN2A variants (p.Gly35Ala, p.Gly67Arg, p.Glu69Gly, and p.Arg87Trp) bind to CDK4 comparably to wild type p16INK4a, but do not inhibit cell proliferation.
source: For example, some CDKN2A variants, such as p.Gly35Ala, p.Gly67Arg, p.Glu69Gly, and p.Arg87Trp, bind to CDK4 comparably to wild type (WT) p16INK4a, but do not inhibit cell proliferation, indicating that additional functions not assessed in vitro CDK4 binding are important for cellular function (Kannengiesser et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Kannengiesser et al., 2009.

claim: PANC-1 is a human PDAC cell line with a homozygous deletion of CDKN2A.
source: PANC-1 (CRL-1469) is a human PDAC cell line with a homozygous deletion of CDKN2A (Caldas et al., 1994).
evidence: This is cited from Caldas et al., 1994.

claim: CDKN2A (p16INK4A) was not detectable in PANC-1 cells by western blot.
source: Consistent with previous reports, CDKN2A (p16INK4A) was not detectable in PANC-1 cells by western blot (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: Stable expression of WT CDKN2A in PANC-1 cells resulted in a significant reduction in cell proliferation compared to empty vector control (p-value < 0.0001).
source: Stable expression of WT CDKN2A in PANC-1 cells through lentiviral transduction resulted in a significant reduction in cell proliferation compared to empty vector control (p-value < 0.0001) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Stable expression of pathogenic CDKN2A variants (p.Leu78Hisfs*41, p.Gly101Trp, or p.Val126Asp) in PANC-1 cells resulted in no reduction in cell proliferation compared to the empty vector control.
source: Conversely, stable expression of three known pathogenic, and therefore functionally deleterious, CDKN2A variants, p. Leu78Hisfs*41, p.Gly101Trp, or p.Val126Asp, in PANC-1 cells resulted in no reduction in cell proliferation compared to the empty vector control (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean cell proliferation value for all pathogenic variants assayed was 0.90 (range: 0.84–1.03).
source: The mean cell proliferation value for all pathogenic variants assayed was 0.90 (range: 0.84–1.03), while the mean cell proliferation value for all benign variants assayed was 0.26 (range: 0.14–0.48) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is calculated from the cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mean cell proliferation value for all benign variants assayed was 0.26 (range: 0.14–0.48).
source: The mean cell proliferation value for all pathogenic variants assayed was 0.90 (range: 0.84–1.03), while the mean cell proliferation value for all benign variants assayed was 0.26 (range: 0.14–0.48) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is calculated from the cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was clear demarcation between the mean cell proliferations values of assayed benchmark pathogenic and benign variants.
source: Importantly, there was clear demarcation between the mean cell proliferations values of assayed benchmark pathogenic and benign variants.
evidence: This is observed from the cell proliferation data and is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eleven of the 29 VUSs (37.9%) had cell proliferation scores above 0.81 and were classified as functionally deleterious.
source: Eleven of the 29 VUSs (37.9%) had cell proliferation scores above 0.81 and were classified as functionally deleterious, including p.Thr18Pro, p.Ala20Gly, p.Gln50Arg, p.His66Pro, p.Ala68Val, p.Asp74Ala,, p.Asp84Ala, p.Gly89Asp, p.Ala109Pro, p.Ala127Pro, and p.Arg128Pro.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the functional assay performed in this study.

claim: One VUS (3.4%), p.Leu65Pro, had a cell proliferation score between 0.66 and 0.81 and was classified as potentially functionally deleterious.
source: One VUS (3.4%), p.Leu65Pro, had a cell proliferation score between 0.66 and 0.81 and was classified as potentially functionally deleterious.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the functional assay performed in this study.

claim: Three VUSs (10.3%), p.Asp74His, p.Gly111Ser, and p.Gly122Val, had a cell proliferation score between 0.66 and 0.44 and were classified as potentially functionally neutral.
source: Three VUSs (10.3%), p.Asp74His, p.Gly111Ser, and, p.Gly122Val, had a cell proliferation score between 0.66 and 0.44 and were classified as potentially functionally neutral.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the functional assay performed in this study.

claim: Fourteen VUSs (48.3%) had cell proliferation scores below 0.44 and were classified as functionally neutral.
source: The remaining 14 VUSs (48.3%) had cell proliferation scores below 0.44 and were classified as functionally neutral, including p.Met9Thr, p.Pro11Leu, p.Arg24Gln, p.Pro41Gln, p.His66Arg, p.Gly67Arg, p.Glu69Gly, p.Arg99Gly, p.Gly101Arg, p.Arg124Cys, p.Asp125His, p.Ala134Thr, p.Gly139Arg, p.Ala143Thr.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the functional assay performed in this study.

claim: MIA PaCa-2 and AsPC-1 are PDAC cell lines with homozygous deletions of CDKN2A.
source: To determine if the PDAC cell line used in our assay affected variant functional characterizations, we assayed all CDKN2A variants (benchmark pathogenic, benchmark benign, and VUS) using two additional PDAC cell lines with homozygous deletions of CDKN2A: MIA PaCa-2 (ATCC, catalog no. CRL-1420) and AsPC-1 (ATCC, catalog no. CRL-1682) (Yamato and Furukawa, 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Yamato and Furukawa, 2001.

claim: Western blot did not detect expression of p16INK4A in MIA PaCa-2 and AsPC-1 cell lines.
source: Western blot for CDKN2A did not detect expression of p16INK4A in either cell line (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was clear demarcation between the mean cell proliferation values of assayed benchmark pathogenic and benign variants in both MIA PaCa-2 and AsPC-1.
source: Importantly, there was clear demarcation between the mean cell proliferation values of assayed benchmark pathogenic and benign variants in both MIA PaCa-2 and AsPC-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: In MIA PaCa-2 cells, 7 (24.1%) VUSs were characterized as functionally deleterious.
source: In MIA PaCa-2 cells, 7 (24.1%) VUSs were characterized as functionally deleterious, 5 (17.2%) as potentially functionally deleterious, 3 (10.3%) as potentially functionally neutral, and 14 (48.3%) as functionally neutral based on their mean cell proliferation values (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is from the cell proliferation assay data in MIA PaCa-2 cells.

claim: In AsPC-1 cells, 6 (20.7%) VUSs were characterized as functionally deleterious.
source: In AsPC-1 cells, 6 (20.7%) VUSs were characterized as functionally deleterious, 6 (20.7%) as potentially functionally deleterious, 8 (27.6%) as potentially functionally neutral, and 9 (31%) as functionally neutral based on their mean cell proliferation values (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is from the cell proliferation assay data in AsPC-1 cells.

claim: There was classification agreement between VUS functional classifications across cell lines.
source: Importantly, there was classification agreement between VUS functional classifications across cell lines (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is observed from comparing results across the three cell lines.

claim: The percent of cells in G1 phase for benchmark pathogenic variants (47.2%, range: 43–50.9%) was significantly lower than benchmark benign variants (63.1%, range: 58.4–67.1%) (p-value < 0.01).
source: The percent of cells in G1 phase for benchmark pathogenic variants (47.2%, range: 43–50.9%) and VUSs with functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious classifications (48.5%, range: 42.2–52.3%) were significantly lower than benchmark benign variants (63.1%, range: 58.4–67.1%) (p-value < 0.01, Student's t test) and VUSs with functionally neutral or potentially functionally neutral classifications (62.8%, range: 57.6–68.8%) (p-value < 0.01, Student's t test) (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is from cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The percent of cells in G1 phase for VUSs with functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious classifications (48.5%, range: 42.2–52.3%) was significantly lower than VUSs with functionally neutral or potentially functionally neutral classifications (62.8%, range: 57.6–68.8%) (p-value < 0.01).
source: The percent of cells in G1 phase for benchmark pathogenic variants (47.2%, range: 43–50.9%) and VUSs with functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious classifications (48.5%, range: 42.2–52.3%) were significantly lower than benchmark benign variants (63.1%, range: 58.4–67.1%) (p-value < 0.01, Student's t test) and VUSs with functionally neutral or potentially functionally neutral classifications (62.8%, range: 57.6–68.8%) (p-value < 0.01, Student's t test) (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is from cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The percent of cells in G2/M phase for benchmark pathogenic variants (42.4%, range: 37.7–49.2%) was significantly higher than benchmark benign variants (25.7%, range: 19.3–35.1%) (p-value < 0.01).
source: Similarly, the percent of cells in G2/M phase for benchmark pathogenic variants (42.4%, range: 37.7–49.2%) and VUSs with functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious classifications (40.4%, range: 37.3–45.5%) were significantly lower than benchmark benign variants (25.7%, range: 19.3–35.1%) and VUSs with functionally neutral or potentially functionally neutral classifications (26.6%, range: 18.9–36.6%) (p-value < 0.01, Student's t test) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is from cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: p.Arg24Gln and p.Gly101Arg did not demonstrate deleterious effects in previously reported CDK4 binding and cell proliferation assays.
source: In agreement with our functional classification, p.Arg24Gln and p.Gly101Arg did not demonstrate deleterious effects in previously reported CDK4 binding and cell proliferation assays (Jenkins et al., 2013; Kannengiesser et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies (Jenkins et al., 2013; Kannengiesser et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2011).

claim: p.Gly122Val previously demonstrated CDK6 binding similar to WT CDKN2A, binding to CDK4 was significantly reduced, and partially inhibit cell proliferation.
source: p.Gly122Val previously demonstrated CDK6 binding similar to WT CDKN2A, binding to CDK4 was significantly reduced, and partially inhibit cell proliferation (Yakobson et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Yakobson et al., 2000.

claim: p.Gly67Arg and p.Glu69Gly were previously shown to result in a 40% reduction in CDK4 binding compared to WT CDKN2A.
source: Furthermore, p.Gly67Arg and p.Glu69Gly were previously shown to result in a 40% reduction in CDK4 binding compared to WT CDKN2A (Kannengiesser et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Kannengiesser et al., 2009.

claim: Ten (58.8%) of the 17 CDKN2A VUSs identified in a study of 638 patients with familial pancreatic cancer were found to be functionally deleterious.
source: Ten (58.8%) of the 17 CDKN2A VUSs identified in a study of 638 patients with familial pancreatic cancer (Roberts et al., 2016) were found to be functionally deleterious in our assay and could be reclassified as likely pathogenic variants.
evidence: This is calculated by applying the functional assay results to variants identified in Roberts et al., 2016.

claim: In a study of 727 patients with a family history of PDAC, 6 (46.2%) of 13 CDKN2A VUSs identified were functionally deleterious.
source: In another study of 727 patients with a family history of PDAC, including patients that did not meet the criteria for classification as familial pancreatic cancer, 6 (46.2%) of 13 CDKN2A VUSs identified were functionally deleterious in our assay (Zhen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is calculated by applying the functional assay results to variants identified in Zhen et al., 2015.

claim: In a study of 302 patients with a family history of PDAC, 4 of the 9 (44.4%) CDKN2A VUSs reported were functionally deleterious.
source: Similarly, in a study of 302 patients with a family history of PDAC, 4 of the 9 (44.4%) CDKN2A VUSs reported were functionally deleterious in our assay (Chaffee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is calculated by applying the functional assay results to variants identified in Chaffee et al., 2018.

claim: In a study of 350 patients with PDAC, 3 of 8 (37.5%) VUSs identified were classified as functionally deleterious.
source: When considering patients with PDAC unselected for family history, in one study of 350 patients with PDAC (McWilliams et al., 2018), 3 of 8 (37.5%) VUSs identified were classified as functionally deleterious in our assay.
evidence: This is calculated by applying the functional assay results to variants identified in McWilliams et al., 2018.

claim: In a study of 854 patients with PDAC unselected for family history, the one VUS identified was found to be functionally neutral.
source: On the other hand, in another study of 854 patients with PDAC unselected for family history, the one VUS identified was found to be functionally neutral (Shindo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is calculated by applying the functional assay results to variants identified in Shindo et al., 2017.

claim: The prevalence of likely pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants initially characterized as VUSs is 1.6% (95% CI: 0.8–2.9%) in patients with familial pancreatic cancer.
source: As we assayed all CDKN2A VUSs reported in these studies, our data indicate that the prevalence of likely pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants initially characterized as VUSs is 1.6% (95% CI: 0.8–2.9%) in patients with familial pancreatic cancer, 0.9% (95% CI: 0.5–1.8%) in patients with PDAC positive family history of PDAC (including patients that did not meet the criteria for classification as familial pancreatic cancer), and 0.1% (95% CI: 0.02–0.3%) in PDAC patients unselected for family history.
evidence: This is calculated from the functional assay results applied to published cohorts.

claim: The prevalence of likely pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants initially characterized as VUSs is 0.9% (95% CI: 0.5–1.8%) in patients with PDAC positive family history of PDAC.
source: As we assayed all CDKN2A VUSs reported in these studies, our data indicate that the prevalence of likely pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants initially characterized as VUSs is 1.6% (95% CI: 0.8–2.9%) in patients with familial pancreatic cancer, 0.9% (95% CI: 0.5–1.8%) in patients with PDAC positive family history of PDAC (including patients that did not meet the criteria for classification as familial pancreatic cancer), and 0.1% (95% CI: 0.02–0.3%) in PDAC patients unselected for family history.
evidence: This is calculated from the functional assay results applied to published cohorts.

claim: The prevalence of likely pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants initially characterized as VUSs is 0.1% (95% CI: 0.02–0.3%) in PDAC patients unselected for family history.
source: As we assayed all CDKN2A VUSs reported in these studies, our data indicate that the prevalence of likely pathogenic germline CDKN2A variants initially characterized as VUSs is 1.6% (95% CI: 0.8–2.9%) in patients with familial pancreatic cancer, 0.9% (95% CI: 0.5–1.8%) in patients with PDAC positive family history of PDAC (including patients that did not meet the criteria for classification as familial pancreatic cancer), and 0.1% (95% CI: 0.02–0.3%) in PDAC patients unselected for family history.
evidence: This is calculated from the functional assay results applied to published cohorts.

claim: The cumulative prevalence of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CDKN2A variants increased from 2.5% to 4.1% (95% CI: 2.8–5.9%) in patients with familial pancreatic cancer when incorporating functionally deleterious VUSs.
source: When incorporating functionally deleterious VUSs we have reclassified as likely pathogenic variants with known pathogenic variants in CDKN2A, the cumulative prevalence of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CDKN2A variants in these studies increased from 2.5% to 4.1% (95% CI: 2.8–5.9%) in patients with familial pancreatic cancer, from 1.7% to 2.7% (95% CI: 1.9–3.9%) in patients with PDAC who had a positive for a family history of the disease (including patients that did not meet the criteria for classification as familial pancreatic cancer), and from 0.7% to 1.0% (95% CI: 0.6–1.7%) in PDAC patients unselected for family history.
evidence: This is calculated by combining known pathogenic variants with reclassified VUSs.

claim: The cumulative prevalence of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CDKN2A variants increased from 1.7% to 2.7% (95% CI: 1.9–3.9%) in patients with PDAC who had a positive family history when incorporating functionally deleterious VUSs.
source: When incorporating functionally deleterious VUSs we have reclassified as likely pathogenic variants with known pathogenic variants in CDKN2A, the cumulative prevalence of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CDKN2A variants in these studies increased from 2.5% to 4.1% (95% CI: 2.8–5.9%) in patients with familial pancreatic cancer, from 1.7% to 2.7% (95% CI: 1.9–3.9%) in patients with PDAC who had a positive for a family history of the disease (including patients that did not meet the criteria for classification as familial pancreatic cancer), and from 0.7% to 1.0% (95% CI: 0.6–1.7%) in PDAC patients unselected for family history.
evidence: This is calculated by combining known pathogenic variants with reclassified VUSs.

claim: The cumulative prevalence of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CDKN2A variants increased from 0.7% to 1.0% (95% CI: 0.6–1.7%) in PDAC patients unselected for family history when incorporating functionally deleterious VUSs.
source: When incorporating functionally deleterious VUSs we have reclassified as likely pathogenic variants with known pathogenic variants in CDKN2A, the cumulative prevalence of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CDKN2A variants in these studies increased from 2.5% to 4.1% (95% CI: 2.8–5.9%) in patients with familial pancreatic cancer, from 1.7% to 2.7% (95% CI: 1.9–3.9%) in patients with PDAC who had a positive for a family history of the disease (including patients that did not meet the criteria for classification as familial pancreatic cancer), and from 0.7% to 1.0% (95% CI: 0.6–1.7%) in PDAC patients unselected for family history.
evidence: This is calculated by combining known pathogenic variants with reclassified VUSs.

claim: Functionally deleterious CDKN2A VUSs are likely to play a significant and previously unappreciated role in risk of PDAC, particularly for patients with a family history of the disease.
source: Regardless, we can conclude that functionally deleterious CDKN2A VUSs are likely to play a significant and previously unappreciated role in risk of PDAC, particularly for patients with a family history of the disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the prevalence data and functional characterization results.

claim: VUS functional characterizations were generally consistent when using PANC-1, MIA PaCA-2, and AsPC-1 cells in the cell proliferation assay.
source: VUS functional characterizations were generally consistent when using PANC-1, MIA PaCA-2, and AsPC-1 cells in our cell proliferation assay.
evidence: This is observed from comparing results across the three cell lines.

claim: No variant found to be functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious when assayed with one cell line had a functionally neutral or potentially functionally neutral classification when assayed with another cell line.
source: Specifically, no variant found to be functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious when assayed with one cell line, had a functionally neutral or potentially functionally neutral classification when assayed with another cell line.
evidence: This is observed from comparing results across the three cell lines.

claim: PDAC cell lines had different genetic alterations and degrees of ploidy.
source: Furthermore, PDAC cell lines had different genetic alterations and degrees of ploidy (Sirivatanauksorn et al., 2001; Yamato and Furukawa, 2001) indicating that our functional classifications are robust to cell line-specific effects.
evidence: This is cited from Sirivatanauksorn et al., 2001 and Yamato and Furukawa, 2001.

claim: Benchmark pathogenic variants and VUSs classified as functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious had a significantly lower percent of cells in G1 phase compared to benchmark benign variants or VUSs classified as functionally benign or potentially functionally benign.
source: Consistent with our functional classifications, we found that benchmark pathogenic variants and VUSs classified as functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious had a significantly lower percent of cells in G1 phase and a significantly higher percent of cells in G2/M phase of the cell cycle compared to either benchmark benign variants or VUSs classified as functionally benign or potentially functionally benign.
evidence: This is from cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Benchmark pathogenic variants and VUSs classified as functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious had a significantly higher percent of cells in G2/M phase compared to benchmark benign variants or VUSs classified as functionally benign or potentially functionally benign.
source: Consistent with our functional classifications, we found that benchmark pathogenic variants and VUSs classified as functionally deleterious or potentially functionally deleterious had a significantly lower percent of cells in G1 phase and a significantly higher percent of cells in G2/M phase of the cell cycle compared to either benchmark benign variants or VUSs classified as functionally benign or potentially functionally benign.
evidence: This is from cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Expression of CDKN2A variants classified as pathogenic, functionally deleterious, or potentially functionally deleterious do not control progression through the cell cycle.
source: These data suggest that expression of CDKN2A variants classified as pathogenic, functionally deleterious, or potentially functionally deleterious do not control progression through the cell cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle analysis data.

claim: Reintroduction of CDKN2A into cancer cells lacking CDKN2A delays cell cycle progression.
source: As reintroduction of CDKN2A into cancer cells lacking CDKN2A delays cell cycle progression, we determined the percent of variant-expressing PANC-1 cells in G1, G2/M, and S phases of the cell cycle (Miller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Miller et al., 2011.

claim: The assay of broad cellular function may encompass functions other than CDK4 binding.
source: First, our assay is of broad cellular function, specifically cell proliferation, and therefore, may encompass functions other than CDK4 binding.
